All teams ↗

Answer routine help from the runbook

Employees often ask IT in Slack before opening a ticket. Nema can use an approved runbook to answer a routine question, cite the relevant step, and collect the details needed when self-service does not solve the problem.

Start with a narrow topic such as VPN access, device setup, or a common application error. The answer should name the runbook version and keep any account-specific information in an appropriate channel.

Turn a message into useful intake

Give Nema the service desk's required fields and routing rules. It can ask for the device, operating system, error text, business impact, urgency, and troubleshooting already attempted. The result is a structured request that saves the technician from repeating intake.

Nema can suggest a queue and owner based on the team's rules. IT reviews the destination and any proposed ticket creation. Unusual requests remain visible rather than being forced into a familiar category.

Prepare access requests

Access work requires more than identifying the application. Nema can collect the requester, target system, requested role, business reason, duration, manager or resource owner, and policy references. It can then prepare an approval packet.

The system owner or authorized approver decides whether to grant access. Nema should not reset an account, change a role, or bypass an approval because the request sounds routine. When a supported action exists, show the exact proposed change.

Carry incident context across shifts

During an incident, Nema can organize the Slack thread into a timeline, known impact, checks completed, active hypotheses, current owners, and next actions. Source links let the incoming responder inspect the original evidence.

The incident lead owns diagnosis and remediation. A clean handoff reduces repeated work while keeping uncertain causes clearly labeled. Afterward, the same timeline can help draft a runbook update for the owner to review.

Find repeated help gaps

Provide a bounded set of internal tickets and the current knowledge base. Nema can group recurring questions, identify articles that are missing or inconsistent, and prepare an outline for the service owner. This connects day-to-day requests with documentation work.

The owner decides which pattern deserves a new article and verifies the guidance. Ticket examples should exclude details that the article's broader audience should not see.

Start with one supported service

Choose a common help request and include one case the runbook does not cover. Verify that Nema cites the right steps, collects the missing diagnostics, and routes the exception. Then inspect the ticket payload before approving creation.

Once the request has an owner, Nema can prepare a concise recap for the employee with the ticket link, expected next step, and any safe self-service action. The technician edits that message when the issue needs more context or a different service expectation.

Questions from IT teams

Can Nema reset accounts?

Only when an exact action is supported and your policy allows it. Privileged changes should remain visible to an authorized approver.

Which service desk tools can Nema use?

Connection availability varies by setup. You can prepare the first intake packet with a supplied ticket template before enabling a live create action.

Can Nema work from our runbooks?

Yes. Provide the approved versions and owners, then require citations so employees and technicians can inspect the source.
